documents.title: Syllabus Guidance for Generative AI
documents.summary: The Center for Teaching and Learning tells faculty to state their own generative AI expectations, suggests three use levels, favors co-creating rules with students, and strongly encourages RIT-supported tools. It then reproduces faculty syllabus examples (life sciences, two computing, information, cybersecurity, mechanical engineering) ranging from limited use to expected use.
documents.stance_why: The page sets no single rule: "Approaches to generative AI course policy and syllabus statement development will vary by program, instructor, course, assessment" and offers "three acceptable use levels" (No AI use, Some AI use with restrictions, Open use of AI), so the decision is handed to instructors and tiers are listed.

units.why: The page says 'GenAI technology is incredibly dynamic and constantly evolving', acknowledging that rules must change; P54 is nearest.
units.anchor: incredibly dynamic and constantly evolving
units.fit_note: Notes the technology evolves and teaching needs agility; no commitment to review a policy.
units.resolution_why: Coder A did not code this passage. The source says: "incredibly dynamic and constantly evolving". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder B's codes.

units.why: The intro states the resource 'is intended to help faculty begin to address generative AI in RIT course policies and syllabi', a statement of purpose and scope, P56.
units.anchor: intended to help faculty begin to address generative AI in RIT course policies
units.resolution_why: Coder A did not code this passage. The source says: "intended to help faculty begin to address generative AI in RIT course policies". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder B's codes.

units.why: The Center for Teaching and Learning "strongly encourages the use of RIT-supported AI tools", a university-level recommendation to prefer sanctioned tools, so it is a sanctioned-tool policy (P17) rather than a generic permit.
units.anchor: strongly encourages the use of RIT-supported AI tools
units.fit_note: Encourages use of vetted institutional tools in general; does not say the university provides one course tool. / The encouragement is aimed at faculty, not a tool a course provides.
units.resolution_why: The CTL sentence encourages everyone to use RIT-supported tools; it is not addressed only to instructors, so I keep coder A's all/general rather than B's instructor/before-course.

units.why: The same sentence asks faculty "to clearly articulate their expectations for generative AI use", a request that instructors communicate AI rules; P09 fits since it concerns stating expectations in course policies.
units.anchor: for RIT faculty to clearly articulate their expectations for generative AI use in the classroom
units.policy: The Center for Teaching and Learning strongly encourages RIT faculty to clearly articulate their expectations for generative AI use in the classroom.
units.fit_note: Strongly encouraged, not required, and not limited to the syllabus.

units.why: Faculty are told to "clarify for yourself what the role of generative AI should be in your class", so the role of AI is decided by the individual instructor, which is P04.
units.anchor: clarify for yourself what the role of generative AI should be in your class

units.why: The page says "the landscape will continue to change", acknowledging the guidance is provisional; P54 is the nearest type though it promises no review.
units.anchor: keeping in mind that the landscape will continue to change
units.fit_note: Notes that the AI landscape will change; no review cycle or feedback mechanism is stated.
units.resolution_why: Coder B did not code this passage. The source says: "keeping in mind that the landscape will continue to change". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder A's codes.

units.why: The source says it "can also be helpful to check with colleagues in your department to see how they are addressing generative AI", an optional suggestion to faculty before designing a course policy; peer consultation is the nearest to supporting faculty in learning AI.
units.anchor: check with colleagues in your department to see how they are addressing generative AI
units.fit_note: Instructors may look at how departmental colleagues handle AI when setting their own policy. / Peer consultation within the department, not workshops or training.
units.resolution_why: A coded may/UNCOVERED, B coded should/P63. The source says "it can also be helpful", which is optional (may, not should). Peer consultation is a form of faculty learning support, so P63 with a fit_note is better than UNCOVERED.

units.why: "Approaches ... will vary by program, instructor, course, assessment, and even by individual learning activities" says no single rule exists and the decision is local: P04.
units.anchor: will vary by program, instructor, course, assessment, and even by individual learning activities

units.why: The page offers "three acceptable use levels" (No AI use, Some AI use with restrictions, Open use of AI), which are named tiers: P05.
units.anchor: outlining three acceptable use levels
units.policy: Instructors may outline expectations in the syllabus and classroom as three acceptable use levels: no AI use, some AI use with restrictions, and open use of AI.

units.why: It warns that 'a blanket statement prohibiting the use of generative AI can result in an adversarial situation'. This advises against a blanket ban; no type covers that, and P03 is about discouraging AI itself, so UNCOVERED.
units.anchor: a blanket statement prohibiting the use of generative AI can result in an adversarial situation
units.uncovered_note: Advises against a blanket prohibition because it can create an adversarial climate; a caution about framing rather than a rule on AI use. / Advises instructors against a blanket ban on generative AI because it creates an adversarial classroom.
units.resolution_why: A coded P66 permit, B coded UNCOVERED neutral. The source warns that "a blanket statement prohibiting the use of generative AI can result in an adversarial situation"; it says nothing about explaining rules to students, so P66 is stretched. UNCOVERED and neutral (advice, not a rule on AI use itself).

units.why: "faculty may wish to co-create expectations for the use of generative AI with students" names co-creating the AI rules with students, which is P67.
units.anchor: faculty may wish to co-create expectations for the use of generative AI with students
units.resolution_why: Phase: co-creating the expectations is part of policy design, so before-course (A) rather than course-start (B). unit_stance neutral (B): the sentence is about procedure, not a position on AI use.

units.why: Faculty 'may also consider communicating their expectations... within individual assignment instructions, during course discussion, and within learning activities'. This extends communication beyond the syllabus; P66 fits better than P09, which is about the syllabus statement.
units.anchor: communicating their expectations for generative AI use within individual assignment instructions
units.fit_note: Optional, and extends to course discussion and learning activities as well as the syllabus and assignment instructions. / Concerns channels for communicating the rule, not explaining reasons.
units.resolution_why: A coded P09 (every syllabus needs a statement), B coded P66. The source says faculty may communicate expectations "within individual assignment instructions, during course discussion, and within learning activities", which is about explaining rules, not requiring a syllabus statement. P66.

units.why: "Clearly communicating your expectations to students can reduce confusion ... and promote academic integrity" gives the reason for explaining the rules, P66.
units.anchor: Clearly communicating your expectations to students can reduce confusion
units.fit_note: Gives the benefit of clear communication; does not discuss reasons behind particular AI rules.
units.resolution_why: A coded P66, B coded P09. The sentence says clear communication "can reduce confusion ... and promote academic integrity", a rationale for explaining rules to students, so P66 (A); P09 is about requiring a syllabus statement.

units.why: The School of Life Sciences example says students "are encouraged to explore the use of RIT-supported generative artificial intelligence tools" for data analysis and writing, an encouraging default (P02).
units.anchor: students are encouraged to explore the use of RIT-supported generative artificial intelligence tools

units.why: "any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited" is a must-level disclosure requirement: P24.
units.anchor: any such use must be appropriately acknowledged and cited

units.why: The example says acknowledgements "can be done via in-text citations, quotations, or references ... and comments in data analysis submissions", specifying where to mark AI use, closest to P27.
units.anchor: comments in data analysis submissions or paper discussions
units.policy: Acknowledgements of AI use can be made via in-text citations, quotations, or references in writing assignments, and comments in data analysis submissions or paper discussions.
units.fit_note: Covers in-text citations in prose as well as comments in data analysis; not only AI-derived code. / Also allows in-text citation in prose, not only code comments.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance: A neutral, B require. The source says acknowledgement "can be done via" in-text citations or comments, which lists acceptable forms; it requires nothing new (the requirement is the previous sentence), so neutral.

units.why: "Violations of this policy will be considered as academic misconduct" classifies breaches as misconduct: P36.
units.anchor: Violations of this policy will be considered as academic misconduct

units.why: "It is your responsibility to assess the validity of any output generated by AI" tells students to verify AI output: P31.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to assess the validity of any output generated by AI

units.why: The example calls AI output "a starting point" that "rarely accomplishes the tasks to the level expected" and says "thorough modifications are highly recommended"; students should not submit AI output as is, which is P32 (AI does not replace their work) rather than P31 because the point is modification, not error checking.
units.anchor: thorough modifications are highly recommended when making use of these tools
units.fit_note: Recommends heavily modifying AI output; frames AI as a starting point. / Recommends heavy editing of AI output as a starting point; not about the primary problem-solver role.

units.why: 'For the work that you submit, you bear the final responsibility' is student ownership, P29.
units.anchor: For the work that you submit, you bear the final responsibility
units.resolution_why: Phase: A general, B during-work. The sentence concerns the work students submit, so during-work.

units.why: The instructor's framing, "that means learning to use new technologies effectively but also responsibly", explains why the course teaches AI use; it is a rationale (informs) that teaches AI use as a professional skill (P44).
units.anchor: learning to use new technologies effectively but also responsibly
units.resolution_why: A coded student/course-start, B all/general. The passage is a rationale addressed to "you" (students) in a syllabus, so student; a rationale of principle is phase general, not course-start.

units.why: "you are encouraged to work with generative AI tools in ways that let you practice good habits and that help you learn" is an encouraging default with a learning purpose: P02.
units.anchor: you are encouraged to work with generative AI tools in ways that let you practice

units.why: "we do not want generative AI tools to do your work" states the limit on the encouragement; worded as a preference, not a ban, it targets AI producing submitted work, P19.
units.anchor: we do not want generative AI tools to do your work
units.resolution_why: Modality and stance: A coded should-not/restrict, B must-not/prohibit. The wording is "we do not want generative AI tools to do your work", a stated wish within a policy that permits other uses, so should-not and restrict (A).

units.why: "Think about chat-based AI tools like a TA or classmate" treats AI as a human collaborator under existing rules: P45.
units.anchor: Think about chat-based AI tools like a TA or classmate

units.why: Listing "Smart in-context code completion such as GitHub Copilot" as "Acceptable/encouraged" permits AI built into the editor: P07 fits better than P16 because the rule is about completion tools.
units.anchor: Smart in-context code completion such as GitHub Copilot
units.fit_note: Permits and encourages editor code completion (the opposite of requiring students to disable it); that the tool is free for students is also noted. / Also covers editor-integrated completion and a duty to verify the generated code.
units.resolution_why: Type: A P07, B P16. The rule is about in-editor code completion such as Copilot, which is what P07 covers; the condition for using generated code (reading and checking it) is a separate unit. P07 with fit_note. Stance encourage (heading "Acceptable/encouraged").

units.why: The example continues "You read what is generated and confirm that it makes sense and works as intended", a verification duty on generated code: P31.
units.anchor: You read what is generated and confirm that it makes sense and works as intended
units.resolution_why: Coder B did not code this sentence. The source says "you read what is generated and confirm that it makes sense and works as intended", a condition on using generated code, so it is kept (verification, P31).

units.why: "Having a conversation with a chat-based LLM ... about high-level concepts. Asking it to explain a specific snippet of code" lists acceptable tutor-style uses: P12.
units.anchor: Having a conversation with a chat-based LLM (such as ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, etc.) about high-level
units.resolution_why: A's anchor spans two list items. I aligned A with B's first item (conversation about high-level concepts), type P12 (AI as tutor); the second item is a separate B-only unit. The list is headed "Acceptable/encouraged", so unit_stance encourage (A) rather than permit (B).

units.why: It permits 'Asking it to explain a specific snippet of code (one or two functions, say)'. Explaining code to understand it fits P13 better than P12.
units.anchor: Asking it to explain a specific snippet of code (one or two functions, say)
units.fit_note: Explaining code snippets rather than error messages.
units.resolution_why: Coder A merged this list item into the previous unit's anchor. The source lists "asking it to explain a specific snippet of code" separately as acceptable; kept as its own unit. Type P12 (A's choice for the sibling items) rather than B's P13, since explaining code is for understanding, not debugging errors.

units.why: "Asking it to quiz you on course topics" is an allowed study use: P14.
units.anchor: Asking it to quiz you on course topics
units.resolution_why: unit_stance: A encourage, B permit. The list is headed "acceptable/encouraged", so encourage.

units.why: 'you take ultimate responsibility for the integrity of the code you submit' is student ownership, P29.
units.anchor: you take ultimate responsibility for the integrity of the code you submit
units.resolution_why: Phase: A general, B during-work. The sentence concerns the code students submit, so during-work (consistent with the unit on final responsibility).

units.why: Listing "Sharing an account on a Chat model site with another student" as disallowed is a rule about account sharing that no type covers.
units.anchor: Sharing an account on a Chat model site with another student
units.uncovered_note: Students may not share an account on a chat model site with another student. / Students may not share an account on a chat AI site with another student.

units.why: "Uploading/pasting large sections of assignments with the intent of having the AI complete a portion" forbids feeding the assignment to AI: P20.
units.anchor: Uploading/pasting large sections of assignments with the intent of having the AI complete a portion
units.fit_note: Prohibited when the intent is to have the AI complete part of the assignment; large sections are specified. / The ban is limited to large sections pasted with intent to have AI complete work.

units.why: 'it is good practice to try out that code and try to understand how it works' asks students to understand generated code, P30.
units.anchor: good practice to try out that code and try to understand how it works
units.resolution_why: Coder A did not code this passage. The source says: "good practice to try out that code and try to understand how it works". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder B's codes.

units.why: "it is bad practice to 'merely copy/paste' without understanding" asks students to understand AI-generated code before using it: P30.
units.anchor: it is bad practice to "merely copy/paste" without understanding

units.why: "All assignments include a required 'Collaboration and Generative AI disclosure' statement" requires disclosure with each submission: P24.
units.anchor: All assignments include a required “Collaboration and Generative AI disclosure” statement

units.why: "you are required to include a link to your chat history ... or paste in a transcript of the conversation" requires submitting transcripts: P26.
units.anchor: you are required to include a link to your chat history (if available) or paste

units.why: "Cases we deem to be disallowed ... misuse of generative AI will result in a discussion with the instructor" sets a first step of talking with the student: P57.
units.anchor: misuse of generative AI will result in a discussion with the instructor
units.resolution_why: Modality: A must, B informs. "will result in a discussion with the instructor" commits the instructor to a procedure, so must for the instructor actor (A).

units.why: "Repeat offenses may result in grade penalties" states a penalty for repeated misuse, escalating by offense: P37.
units.anchor: Repeat offenses may result in grade penalties
units.fit_note: Penalty is only stated as grade penalties for repeat offenses, with no specific amount.

units.why: "This policy is subject to change, but always as a result of discussion between instructor and students, never as a surprise" is a commitment on how the policy will change: P54.
units.anchor: This policy is subject to change, but always as a result of discussion between instructor
units.fit_note: Also commits that changes follow discussion with students.

units.why: "We will be using ChatGPT (or equivalent) to help develop course materials" discloses that AI-made course materials are used: P48.
units.anchor: We will be using ChatGPT (or equivalent) to help develop course materials
units.fit_note: Discloses AI use in making materials; does not state a review step.

units.why: The instructor says he "uses GitHub Copilot for his own daily coding, but he always carefully examines the outputs", disclosing his own AI use: P47.
units.anchor: Prof. Lange uses GitHub Copilot for his own daily coding

units.why: The definition says "Generative AI refers to a type of artificial intelligence tools that accept user requests as prompts and generate content", fixing what the course policy covers: P61.
units.anchor: accept user requests as prompts and generate content accordingly
units.fit_note: The list includes OS-integrated assistants and IDE completion tools.

units.why: The scope list names "Large language model-powered code completion tools: GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI Assistant" and OS "AI features in Microsoft Windows", extending the policy to editor and OS AI: P07.
units.anchor: Large language model-powered code completion tools: GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI Assistant
units.fit_note: A scope definition naming code completion and OS assistants; no instruction to disable them is stated here.
units.resolution_why: Coder B did not code this passage. The source says: "Large language model-powered code completion tools: GitHub Copilot, JetBrains AI Assistant". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder A's codes.

units.why: 'you may use generative AI to do anything you are allowed to do with another person' is the same analogy as a permission, P45.
units.anchor: you may use generative AI to do anything you are allowed to do with another
units.resolution_why: Coder A coded only the second clause of this sentence. The source's first clause, "you may use generative AI to do anything you are allowed to do with another person", is a distinct permission, so it is kept (may, permit, P45).

units.why: "the rule of thumb is to treat it as if it were a human ... things you are prohibited from doing with another person cannot be done with generative AI either" is the human-collaborator rule: P45.
units.anchor: things you are prohibited from doing with another person cannot be done with generative AI
units.resolution_why: Coder B coded this sentence's first clause (may use AI for anything allowed with another person) but not this second clause: "things you are prohibited from doing with another person cannot be done with generative AI either". It is a separate rule, so it is kept.

units.why: Under "Permitted Actions", "Asking generative AI about a concept in this course" is a tutor-style use: P12.
units.anchor: Asking generative AI about a concept in this course per se

units.why: Prohibiting "Attempting to prompt generative AI to get solutions or reusable code for an assignment or an exam question" bars having AI produce the work: P19.
units.anchor: Attempting to prompt generative AI to get solutions or reusable code for an assignment or

units.why: The same sentence prohibits "adding any amount of assignment instructions and starter code to the prompt", a separate rule about feeding specs and code to AI: P20.
units.anchor: adding any amount of assignment instructions and starter code to the prompt

units.why: "Representing any amount of generative AI output as if it were your own work ... Neither the verbatim output nor any derivation of it is allowed" bans submitting AI output as own work: P19.
units.anchor: Representing any amount of generative AI output as if it were your own work

units.why: "Having generative AI check any work you submit for grading" is prohibited, matching the ban on using AI to check graded work: P21.
units.anchor: Having generative AI check any work you submit for grading

units.why: The rationale says AI output "is not your original work either, so you may not submit it for grading according to the course's Originality of Work requirement", a reason for the ban on submitting AI output: P19.
units.anchor: it is not your original work either, so you may not submit it for grading
units.fit_note: Gives the originality requirement as the reason; the rule is the same as the ban on submitting AI output. / Explains why AI output does not count as the student's own work.
units.resolution_why: A coded must-not P19 prohibit during-work, B informs P29 neutral general. The sentence is inside the rationale but ends in the explicit rule "you may not submit it for grading", so a rule (must-not, prohibit) of type P19, with fit_note that the passage is also the originality rationale.

units.why: "entering your work into generative AI could be effectively equivalent to posting it online" warns that prompts may train the tool and expose student work: P50 (AI tools keep prompts).
units.anchor: entering your work into generative AI could be effectively equivalent to posting it online
units.fit_note: Protects students' own work from training use, not personal data.

units.why: "we reserve the right to require you to explain and/or recreate your work in an in-person, one-on-one meeting" is an oral/in-person check triggered by suspected misuse: P34.
units.anchor: require you to explain and/or recreate your work in an in-person, one-on-one meeting

units.why: "it might output wrong information, so you should use caution and your own judgment" warns students to check AI output: P31.
units.anchor: it might output wrong information, so you should use caution and your own judgment

units.why: "If you have any questions, concerns, or suggestions regarding use of generative AI in this course, please feel free to contact us" invites students to ask; P10 is closest though it does not say to ask before using.
units.anchor: please feel free to contact us
units.fit_note: Invites questions and suggestions but does not tell students to ask before using AI. / Invites questions and suggestions generally, not asking before using AI.

units.why: The School of Information System Administration example states students "are allowed and encouraged to utilize Generative AI tools as a resource for completing assignments": P02.
units.anchor: you are allowed and encouraged to utilize Generative AI tools as a resource for completing

units.why: 'these resources are not a replacement for your learning and comprehension' keeps the student as primary learner, P32.
units.anchor: these resources are not a replacement for your learning and comprehension
units.resolution_why: A coded should-not/during-work, B informs/general. The sentence "these resources are not a replacement for your learning and comprehension" is an explanatory caveat, not an instruction, so informs/general (B).

units.why: Reason given: 'Real-world situations often require quick thinking... without external aids'. Unassisted exams check foundations; P42 (fundamentals first) is nearest.
units.anchor: to accurately assess your understanding and readiness
units.fit_note: The reason is readiness for professional settings without aids.
units.resolution_why: Coder A did not code this passage. The source says: "to accurately assess your understanding and readiness". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder B's codes.

units.why: "all quizzes, exams, and the final practical ... will be conducted without Internet access, meaning you cannot use Generative AI tools" bans AI in assessments: P22.
units.anchor: all quizzes, exams, and the final practical for this course will be conducted without Internet

units.why: The instructor says exams are closed to AI "ensuring that you are building a solid foundational understanding of the course material", a rationale that fundamentals come first (P42), addressed to students and stated as a principle (general).
units.anchor: building a solid foundational understanding of the course material
units.resolution_why: A coded P41/student/course-start, B P42/all/general. The passage is about securing foundational understanding, i.e. fundamentals first (P42), not about shortcuts hurting practice (P41); addressed to "you" so student; rationale so general.

units.why: The instructor's goal "to best prepare you for future professional scenarios where you might not always have immediate access to external resources" is a rationale for the exam rule, tied to professional skills (P44).
units.anchor: prepare you for future professional scenarios where you might not always have immediate access
units.fit_note: A professional-preparation rationale for unassisted assessment, not for learning to use AI. / Prepares students for settings without AI access.
units.resolution_why: A coded student/course-start, B all/general. Addressed to "you" (student); a rationale is phase general. Type P44 with fit_note: the rationale is about working without tools, not teaching AI use.

units.why: "the work you submit will be your own, even when using AI tools to assist" requires submitted work to be the student's own: P29.
units.anchor: the work you submit will be your own, even when using AI tools to assist

units.why: It refers students to 'the department’s academic dishonesty policy' for external-resource use, P36.
units.anchor: refer to the department’s academic dishonesty policy
units.fit_note: Only points to the existing dishonesty policy.
units.resolution_why: Coder A did not code this passage. The source says: "refer to the department’s academic dishonesty policy". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder B's codes.

units.why: The preface says the course will 'introduce cybersecurity students to real-world uses of GenAI in the field', teaching AI as a professional skill, P44.
units.anchor: introduce cybersecurity students to real-world uses of GenAI in the field
units.resolution_why: A coded phase course-start, B general. The line is the preface describing the course aim, background not an expectation, so general.

units.why: The Cybersecurity course statement sets "the expectation in this class is that you use Gen AI tools as much as possible", making AI use expected, so P02 (expects) with a fit note since it goes as far as requiring.
units.anchor: the expectation in this class is that you use Gen AI tools as much as
units.fit_note: Goes beyond allowing or encouraging: AI use is expected in all work. / Use is required, beyond permitted or encouraged.

units.why: "'Cheating,' in this class, may constitute not using enough Gen AI in your work" defines too little AI use as cheating, which no type covers.
units.anchor: may constitute not using enough Gen AI in your work
units.uncovered_note: Not using enough generative AI can itself count as cheating in this course. / Not using enough generative AI counts as cheating in a course that requires AI use.
units.resolution_why: Phase: A general, B when-misuse. The sentence redefines "cheating" for this course; it is a definition, so general, and no sanction is stated.

units.why: "include your own actual observations and reflections in your self-reflection submissions" requires reflections that are the student's own while AI may enhance them; P26 (reflections) is nearest but this is about authentic content.
units.anchor: include your own actual observations and reflections in your self-reflection submissions
units.fit_note: Self-reflections are required and must contain the student's own observations; AI may be used to enhance them. / Requires the student's own reflections, not reflections on AI use.
units.resolution_why: unit_stance: A neutral, B require. The sentence requires students' own reflections but does not require or limit AI use (AI use to enhance them is encouraged), so neutral.

units.why: MECE 200: AI 'may be inaccurate or used in a way that hampers effective concept learning', a warning about accuracy, P31.
units.anchor: provides information that may be inaccurate or used in a way that hampers effective concept
units.fit_note: Also says AI can hamper concept learning. / Also says AI use can hamper concept learning.
units.resolution_why: A coded student/course-start, B all/general. The statement that AI "provides information that may be inaccurate" is a general premise of the policy, not addressed to students in particular, so all/general.

units.why: "The most restrictive is their forbidden use during exams and quizzes" bans AI on assessments: P22.

units.why: "The least restrictive is their use in concept review, studying, and support (excluding content) in the completion of homework assignments" permits AI as a study aid: P14.
units.anchor: their use in concept review, studying, and support (excluding content)

units.why: "being transparent about using AI and submitting work that possesses your original ideas" asks for transparency, a disclosure expectation: P24.
units.anchor: being transparent about using AI
units.fit_note: Also asks that submitted work contain the student's original ideas.
units.resolution_why: Coder B did not code this passage. The source says: "being transparent about using AI". It is a real policy statement, so it is kept with coder A's codes.

units.why: "students are allowed to use AI in limited ways as described further below" is the course default: allowed only for narrow listed uses, so P02 with a note that it is restricted.
units.anchor: students are allowed to use AI in limited ways as described further below
units.fit_note: Default permission is limited to the narrow uses listed, so the stance is closer to restrict. / Permission is narrow and listed, closer to restrict.

units.why: 'AI tools are limited to Google Gemini and Microsoft 365 Copilot. No other AI chatbots are permitted', limits AI to sanctioned tools, P17.
units.anchor: No other AI chatbots are permitted for use with this course
units.fit_note: Limits use to two named RIT-supported tools.

units.why: "Only to formulate alternative meaning to specific engineering topics with the intention of developing deeper understanding" limits AI to concept understanding: P12.
units.anchor: Only to formulate alternative meaning to specific engineering topics

units.why: "Only with proper citations and acknowledgement" makes citation a condition of any AI use: P24.
units.anchor: Only with proper citations and acknowledgement

units.why: "Only for non-graded assignments ... AI will not be used to generate content for graded assignments" bars AI-produced graded work: P19.
units.anchor: AI will not be used to generate content for graded assignments

units.why: "Students are responsible for identifying and addressing any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or problematic AI-generated content" requires verifying AI output: P31.
units.anchor: Students are responsible for identifying and addressing any inaccurate, biased, offensive, or problematic AI-generated content

units.why: "Students must disclose the use of AI in their work including the specific way AI was used, citing the source and the prompt used" requires detailed disclosure of tool and prompt: P25.

documents.title: D08.0 Student Academic Integrity Policy
documents.summary: RIT's university-wide student academic integrity policy mainly sets out definitions of violations, process, hearings and appeals. AI appears twice: unapproved AI methods count as cheating, and AI content used without authorization or citation counts as plagiarism.
documents.stance_why: The policy lists "unapproved artificial intelligence (AI) methods for assignments, exams, or assessments" as cheating and "AI-generated content without authorization or citation" as plagiarism, so AI is banned unless approved or cited, which is restrict.

units.why: The integrity policy lists as cheating 'Using unauthorized materials, sources, or tools, including unapproved artificial intelligence (AI) methods'. That classifies unauthorized AI as cheating, P36.
units.anchor: including unapproved artificial intelligence (AI) methods for assignments, exams, or assessments
units.frag_start: Using unauthorized materials, sources, or tools,
units.fit_note: Also implies AI is banned unless approved, for all assignments, exams and assessments.
units.resolution_why: Phase: A general, B when-misuse. The policy lists unapproved AI use as a kind of cheating, i.e. defines misconduct; the unit is about misconduct, so when-misuse (consistent with the syllabus violation units). unit_stance: unapproved AI use is banned, approved use is allowed, so restrict (A).

units.why: Under plagiarism it lists 'Using AI-generated content without authorization or citation'. Missing authorization or citation is plagiarism, P36; the disclosure aspect is secondary.
units.anchor: Using AI-generated content without authorization or citation
units.fit_note: Also implies AI content must be authorized or cited. / Also implies AI content needs authorization or citation.
units.resolution_why: Same resolution as the previous unit: phase when-misuse, unit_stance restrict (AI-generated content is allowed with authorization or citation).

notes: Reconciled from two coders. Only AI-related provisions of D08.0 were coded; its process, hearing and appeal rules apply to AI cases but do not mention AI. The syllabus guidance page reproduces faculty example statements (Life Sciences, two Computer Science, School of Information, Cybersecurity, Mechanical Engineering); units from these are coded as policies stated in the page and are course-level examples, not university rules. Candidate type: sanctioning AI non-use as misconduct (Cybersecurity example) and account sharing, both UNCOVERED. | Coder B: Syllabus page is university-layer CTL guidance but most units come from faculty sample statements (Lange and Liao CS; Arcoraci iSchool; Cybersecurity; MECE; Life Sciences). Topic codes are my own slugs because AGENT_BRIEF.md was not present. | Reconciler: topics normalised to the shared topic vocabulary (coder B used its own slugs). Three coder-B-only units were dropped: the lead-in 'rule of thumb is to treat it as if it were a human' (restated by the two sub-rules that were kept), the sentence 'the following policy applies to this course' (scope lead-in with no rule), and the resource-list link title 'Equity, Privacy, and Academic Integrity in Generative AI' (navigation).
